original_value: Drug addiction and drug-related crime caused by drug dealing are serious problems for many countries. Such problems have gained urgency in China during recent years. However, there has been no research on the relationship between drug dealing and associated factors and its variation over space at a fine scale, such as the police station management area (PSMA), in China. Based on a seven-year data set obtained in ZG city, China, a geographically weighted Poisson regression (GWPR) model was employed to explore the spatial heterogeneity in the relationship between drug dealing and related risk factors, including social-demographic factors and environmental characteristics. The model results indicated that there were more drug dealings in the socially disorganized areas, typically associated with urban villages and floating population. Spatial accessibility had significant impacts on drug dealing. While the main road showed a negative effect, areas with more branch roads and bus stops tended to attract more drug dealings. Additionally, we found that these relationships were spatially nonstationary across space. This research represents the first in discerning spatial variation of drug dealing within a major Chinese city. These findings not only help policy makers better understand drug dealings from a geographical perspective, but can also help them to develop more targeted local intervention strategies.

result.paraphrase: Drug addiction and drug-related crime stemming from drug trafficking are major challenges in many countries, and they have become increasingly urgent in China in recent years. Yet no study in China has examined how drug trafficking relates to associated factors and how that relationship varies spatially at a fine scale, such as the police station management area (PSMA). Using a seven-year dataset from ZG city, China, this study applied a geographically weighted Poisson regression (GWPR) model to investigate spatial heterogeneity in the link between drug trafficking and risk factors, including social-demographic variables and environmental features. The results showed that drug trafficking was more common in socially disorganized areas, typically linked to urban villages and floating populations. Spatial accessibility also had a significant effect: main roads were negatively associated, whereas areas with more branch roads and bus stops tended to have more drug trafficking. These relationships were also found to be spatially nonstationary. This study is the first to identify spatial variation in drug trafficking within a major Chinese city. Its findings can help policymakers better understand drug trafficking from a geographic perspective and support the design of more targeted local intervention strategies.
